title: Computing Along the Big Long River

source.pdf_page_offset_note: The PDF contains 18 physical pages with matching internal page headers after the cover page.

notes: All 18 UTF-8 page files were read sequentially by the root context.
Fresh read-only visual contexts reviewed all 18 pages using byte-bounded JPEG proxies, one image per tool call, and returned text-only reports.
Visual review reconciled formulas, eleven important figures, dense tables, the missing night-10 row, the ratio reversal, and formatting defects without sending images to the root context.

decisions: which group moves to each open campsite

section_map.summary: The abstract states the scheduling objective, campsite-movement model, daily algorithm, long-run carrying-capacity calculation, Grand Canyon case study, and sensitivity to propulsion, duration, and campsite count.
The introduction moves from scheduling analogies to the 225-mile river, six-month season, wilderness campsite constraint, verification plan, manager memo, and claimed adaptability.
The problem definition asks for a schedule, allowable daily starts, and carrying capacity, then defines carrying capacity as the maximum groups sent during the season.
The overview presents a flexible simulation whose inputs are trip-length distribution, propulsion ratio, and campsite count and whose output is successful six-month trip count.
The paper fixes river length, craft speeds, duration choices, uniform campsites, one group per campsite, downstream motion, daily travel limits, ignored weather, and exact final-day exit.

The notation defines group, trip length, elapsed nights, campsite count and location, current location, scheduled daily distance, maximum daily distance, priority, reachable set, propulsion ratio, duration distribution, current trips, and peak capacity.
The methods define open campsites, movement, waitlist, final exit, the furthest-empty scan, the reachable group set, and a schedule-relative priority score.

Each day the procedure scans empty campsites from downstream to upstream, forms the reachable candidates, selects the highest-priority group, moves it, and applies waitlist, ahead-of-schedule, and final-exit special rules.
Three-group diagrams, a flowchart, a four-group table, and location and priority plots illustrate the daily assignment logic and its repeated behavior.
The hypothetical trace and Grand Canyon sweep connect daily launch rate to completed, late, and waitlisted trips and choose eighteen starts per day as the last zero-late zero-waitlist case.
The case study varies campsites Y, oar-to-motor ratio R, and duration distribution D, tabulates peak carrying capacities, and presents a fitted contour surface.
The conclusion recommends using campsite count, propulsion mix, and duration mix to estimate capacity and proposes an uncalibrated transfer from Grand Canyon results to the Big Long River.
The limitation section acknowledges roughly threefold capacity overestimation, campsite crowding and environmental damage, and omission of river speed and submerged campsites.
Six references provide river-management and scheduling context, but old HTTP links, a dynamic encyclopedia page, and absent archived inputs limit reproducibility.
The memo translates the algorithm and case study into manager-facing guidance about carrying capacity, propulsion ratio, duration mix, and additional trips.

assumptions.summary: The river is 225 miles long, the operating season lasts six months, and campsites are uniformly spaced.
Only oar rafts at 4 mph and motorized boats at 8 mph are modeled.
Durations are restricted to oar trips of 12 or 18 days and motor trips of 6 or 12 days.
At most one group occupies a campsite per night and groups move only downstream or remain in place.
Daily travel occurs between 8am and 6pm with nine effective travel hours after breaks.
Weather, river conditions, campsite closures, and varying flow speed are ignored.
Every group exits exactly on the final day of its intended trip and never early.
The manager can choose the daily oar-to-motor ratio and duration distribution.

data_and_preprocessing.summary: Problem constants provide 225 miles, two craft speeds, a six-month season, and one-group-per-campsite occupancy.
Figure 3.1 gives four hypothetical group traces by night, campsite, and priority.
Figure 4.1 gives completed, late, and waitlisted counts for six through twenty-one groups launched per day.
Figure 4.2 gives capacity for Y in 100, 150, 200, 250, and 300 and five oar-to-motor ratios.
Figure 4.4 gives capacity for five ratios and four duration-distribution scenarios at Y=200.
Six cited web sources provide Grand Canyon and scheduling context but no frozen reproduction inputs.

Represent the simulated peak seasonal capacity as a function of campsite count, propulsion ratio, and duration distribution.
Represent First Launch, Y internal campsites, Final Exit, current groups, and a waitlist in an ordered state array.
Find the furthest open campsite and repeat upstream after every assignment.
Build the candidate groups that can reach the current target without exceeding daily travel.
Choose the highest-priority feasible group for a target campsite.
Treat unlaunched groups as located at First Launch with a special priority value.
Block a group from moving farther than its cumulative schedule target even when physically reachable.
Move eligible groups from their last campsite to an always-open Final Exit state.
Repeat target selection, candidate construction, priority choice, movement, and state update for every open campsite.
Replay four groups and record campsite location and priority by night.
Increase groups launched per day and record completed, late, and waitlisted counts over six months.
For each campsite count and propulsion ratio, raise daily launches until the selected peak-capacity criterion is reached.
At Y=200 vary propulsion ratio and duration distribution and compare peak capacity.

verification.summary: The three-group example can be replayed against reachability and priority selection.
verification.strength: The intended local choice is visible.
verification.limitation: The figure contains a priority-label typo and no tie case.

verification.summary: The flowchart exposes the repeated furthest-empty and highest-priority loop.
verification.limitation: Special waitlist and Final Exit rules are missing.

verification.summary: The four-group table and plots compare location and priority over time.
verification.strength: The traces show qualitative convergence toward schedule.
verification.limitation: The night-10 row is absent and priorities do not all recalculate.

verification.summary: The Grand Canyon sweep identifies eighteen launches per day as the last zero-late zero-waitlist case.
verification.strength: The table preserves all three outcome counts.
verification.limitation: It censors 252 launched groups at season end.

verification.summary: The Y-R grid supports exact column-wise maximum checks.
verification.limitation: The prose universal 1:1 claim has three counterexamples.

verification.summary: The R-D grid supports exact scenario-wise maximum and near-tie checks.
verification.limitation: No repeated-run uncertainty supports the four-trip difference.

verification.summary: The authors compare the model's roughly 3000 trips with a real level near 1000.
verification.limitation: No recalibration or predictive validation follows.

results_trace.summary: The four-group simulation records distinct campsite and priority trajectories over approximately twenty nights.
At eighteen launches per day the table reports 2988 completed, zero late, and zero waitlisted trips.
At nineteen through twenty-one launches per day completions rise but late and waitlisted counts appear.
The Y-R table maxima vary by campsite count rather than remaining universally at R=1:1.
The contour plot suggests a fitted capacity surface but supplies no reproducible fitting model.
The R-D table's global maximum is 2851 at R=4:1 and D=6-12, only four above the 2:1 cell.
The model output near 3000 is roughly three times the cited real Grand Canyon level near 1000.
The memo recommends schedule use and propulsion-duration adjustments but reverses the ratio direction.

judge_relevance_hypotheses.summary: The abstract gives judges a complete map from task through algorithm, case, and sensitivity before details begin.
A compact flowchart can make a simulation inspectable when every special rule and update state is represented.
Exact sensitivity tables are persuasive only when the prose recommendation follows their actual maxima and uncertainty.

weaknesses.summary: The waitlist state has l_i=0, making the printed priority P_i undefined; assigning P=1 is stated informally rather than as a formal piecewise definition.
The printed reachable set G_c omits the downstream condition c>=l_i and therefore can include a campsite upstream of a group's current location.
Tie breaking, waitlist order, state-update timing, a one-move-per-day flag, and fallback after a candidate fails a special rule are not defined.
The literal exit condition t_i=d_i can strand a group forever if it misses that equality day, conflicting with the later existence of late trips.
Several priorities in Figure 3.1 cannot be reproduced stably from the printed formula and displayed state values.
Figure 3.1 jumps from night 9 to night 11 and contains no night-10 row in the source table.
Carrying capacity alternates among launched groups, completed groups, and the highest launch rate with zero late and zero waitlisted trips.
At eighteen groups per day, 3240 groups are launched but only 2988 finish; 252 right-censored groups, 7.78 percent, are not negligible.
Eighteen groups per day is not the largest completed-trip result; it is only the last displayed setting with zero late and zero waitlisted trips.
Figure 4.2 does not support a universal R=1:1 optimum: the maxima are 1:4 at Y=100, 1:1 at Y=150, 1:2 at Y=200 and 250, and 1:1 at Y=300.
Figure 4.4 has different ratio optima by duration distribution: 4:1 for D=12, 2:1 for D=12-18, 4:1 for D=6-12, and 1:2 for D=6-18.
The 2851 versus 2847 difference is only four trips and has no random-error or repeated-run analysis, so 4:1 is not shown to be a robust optimum.
Figure 4.3 supplies no fitted equation, ratio encoding, function family, residuals, uncertainty, or validation.
The transfer rule 3000-X lacks Big Long River values for Y, R, D, environmental capacity, season operations, and empirical calibration.
No code, random seed, repeat count, configuration, stopping rule, fitted surface, or intermediate log is provided.
The memo reverses R from oar: motor in the body to motor:oar, yet repeats a 4:1 recommendation that can therefore be implemented in the opposite direction.
The memo uses optimal, thoroughly tested, ensures, and true wilderness experience beyond the evidence supplied by the simulation.
Figure 2.1 labels Group B's priority as P_A=1.5.
The reachable-set prose uses l_c where l_i is intended, and 'within at least m_i' should be 'within at most m_i'.
Figure 2.4 omits the P=1 waitlist convention and the Final Exit special rule.
The submitted paper retains numerous red spelling and grammar checker underlines in the final visual artifact.
The roughly 3000 modeled trips are about three times the cited real level of roughly 1000 and cannot be used directly as an operating recommendation.

independent_extensions.summary: Write a formal state machine with one-move-per-day flags, deterministic tie breaking, waitlist order, fallback, and atomic daily updates.
Define reachability with both downstream and maximum-distance bounds and define priority piecewise at First Launch.
Replace exact exit equality with a tested completion rule that cannot strand late groups.
Separate launched, completed, censored, late, and queued groups and choose one capacity metric before sweeping launch rate.
Publish code, configuration, seeds, repeat counts, stopping rules, fitted equation, residuals, and machine-readable tables.
Use repeated simulations and uncertainty intervals to distinguish near ties such as 2851 versus 2847.
Calibrate campsite locations, capacities, group sizes, closures, flow, ecology, and season operations to the target river before transfer.
Generate the memo directly from typed model outputs so ratio direction, metric, uncertainty, and caveats cannot drift.
